subject: Francis Ford Coppola
hook: Who bets their own house on a movie?
twist: The vineyard he sold a piece of to fund Megalopolis was first bought with Godfather profits: a film paid for the vines, and the vines paid for a film.
mood: Humid jungle-green and tangerine screenprint mixed with vintage wine-label engraving: cross-hatched vine leaves, banderoles and oval cartouches over misregistered two-colour jungle foliage and a hot tangerine sun. Music: slow, sultry cinematic groove around 80 bpm, with warm Rhodes, upright bass, brushed drums, a distant pedal-steel drone and soft marimba, building to a swelling string pad at the twist.
narration: Who bets their own house on a movie? Francis Ford Coppola did. In nineteen seventy-six, he took his crew to the Philippines to shoot Apocalypse Now. It was meant to cost twelve million dollars. A typhoon hit, and the shoot ran over a year. Newsweek reported he had put up all his own assets as guarantees on the loans. The film won the top prize at Cannes. The bet paid off. Decades later, he did it again. Megalopolis reportedly cost one hundred twenty million dollars, and he funded it himself. He sold part of his wine business to raise it. Here is the quiet part. That wine business began with Godfather profits. A film paid for the vines, and the vines paid for a film. Bold gamble or reckless folly?

fun_facts: Apocalypse Now's principal photography lasted 238 days, from March 1976 to May 1977, against a planned four months (Wikipedia citing Cowie).
At Cannes in 1979 Coppola said: 'We had access to too much money, too much equipment, and little by little we went insane.' (Wikipedia citing Cowie 1990)
Megalopolis grossed roughly 14 million dollars worldwide (Wikipedia); Coppola first conceived the idea around 1977 while finishing Apocalypse Now.

captions.instagram_caption:
Who bets their own house on a movie? 🎬

Francis Ford Coppola did. Making Apocalypse Now in the Philippines (1976-77), he reportedly put up his own assets as guarantees on the loans, while a typhoon and a year-long shoot pushed costs far past the original twelve million dollars.

The film won the top prize at Cannes in 1979, so the bet paid off.

Decades later he did it again. Megalopolis reportedly cost about 120 million dollars, and he funded it himself after selling part of his wine business.

The quiet part: that wine business started with Godfather profits, which helped buy part of Inglenook in Napa Valley. A film paid for the vines, and the vines paid for a film.

question: Bold gamble or reckless folly?
answer: Bold gamble. I love that he backed his own vision, though I'd probably keep the house.
dropped_unverified: Exact 'house' collateral: Newsweek says 'all his own assets'; Wikipedia cites NYT 1981/Biskind for house and car, not fetched, so narration says assets.

Claim that Megalopolis wine money came from Godfather-bought vines: dropped as a direct causal claim; kept only that the wine business began with Godfather profits (CNN) and part was sold (Variety/AP).
Apocalypse gross of 150 million (Eleanor Coppola estimate, single source) and 'twice' bankruptcy talk.
Megalopolis exact budget: reported 120-136 million, hedged as 'reportedly'.
